questions.question: Explain, with the diagram's logic, why an indirect tax raises the equilibrium price by less than the full amount of the tax.
questions.expected_answer: The tax shifts the supply curve leftward (upward by the tax), because sellers must now receive a higher price at every quantity to hand the tax to the state. At the new crossing, price is higher and quantity lower — but as the price rises, buyers cut back along the demand curve, which limits how far the price can climb. The result is that buyers pay part of the tax through a higher price while sellers absorb the rest through a lower net receipt: the burden is shared between the two sides.

questions.question: Compare the side effects of a binding price ceiling and a binding price floor, and explain why each side effect cannot fix itself.
questions.expected_answer: A ceiling below equilibrium creates a permanent shortage: many buyers at the low price, few sellers willing to supply — with queues, informal rationing, black-market sales above the legal price, and falling quality. It cannot fix itself because the rising price that would clear the shortage is illegal. A floor above equilibrium creates a surplus: generous supply but shrunken demand, with unsold stock the state must buy, store, export or watch spoil. It cannot fix itself because the falling price that would clear the surplus is illegal. Ceilings make queues; floors make piles.

questions.question: Present the case for and the case against the minimum wage, and state what the honest conclusion depends on.
questions.expected_answer: For: the unregulated wage for unskilled work can fall below what living costs; the floor protects dignity, reduces working poverty, and the higher wages are spent locally, feeding the circular flow — steadier workers can also be more productive. Against: at the higher cost of labour firms hire fewer workers or mechanise, the crowd of job-seekers grows, the youngest and least skilled are priced out first, and some work moves into the informal shadows without protection. The honest conclusion is a trade-off between protecting the employed and risking the excluded, and its actual size is an empirical question measured in the real world — the diagram gives the shape of the trade-off, not its size.
